title: Show how mass turns flat space into curved spacetime in general relativity: a flat 3D grid of space

scenes.narration: This glowing grid is space around a star. See how the grid lines are pulled in toward it? That’s Einstein’s big idea: mass bends space and time. A ray of light is coming in from the left. First, let’s take the star away. Now the grid is perfectly regular, and the light just goes straight, along the dashed line. Put the star back. Here’s the key: the light still doesn’t turn. It goes as straight as it can. But near the star, straight means following grid lines that bend inward, so the light’s path bends too. It’s like two people walking due north from the equator: both walk straight, yet they meet at the North Pole, because the Earth is curved. In 1919, astronomers saw starlight bend around the Sun just like this. Planets move the same way. Newton says a planet would trace the same oval forever. But in curved spacetime, each lap ends a little further around: the closest point to the star creeps forward, so the orbit slowly draws a flower. Mercury’s orbit really does this. So gravity isn’t a pull. Mass curves spacetime, and light and planets simply move as straight as they can through it.
scenes.visualDescription:
Content needed: Open on a glowing three-dimensional grid bowed inward around a single sphere. Compare a light ray with and without the mass, keeping its incoming direction fixed. Then mark two successive closest approaches on a planet’s rosette. Keep the whole model rotatable.
Notes: Assume the viewer recognizes a straight ray and a planet’s orbit. Use a straight reference line to distinguish what light does locally from where it ends up. The grid is a sketch of curvature, not a material net.
